MUQATIL:12:31-33/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:12:31-33/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:12:31-33/r3.claim: After the women urged him to satisfy her, Joseph preferred prison to adultery; if God did not turn away their schemes, he would yield and become sinful.

FARRA:v2p43/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p43/r2.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p43/r2.claim: السجن means the prison and functions like a verbal noun; a place-name derived from a verb can substitute for the verbal noun, while فتح السين would be an unambiguous verbal noun.

MAJAZ:v1p310/r4.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p310/r4.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p310/r4.claim: Aṣbū ilayhinna means yearning and inclining toward them; Yazīd ibn Ḍabba's verse uses ṣabā for the heart inclining.

MAJAZ:v1p310/r5.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p310/r5.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p310/r5.claim: An anonymous verse uses ṣabā and ṣabwah for longing or inclination.

TAB-FULL:v13p143/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p143/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p143/r1.claim: The report implies the Aziz's wife renewed her seduction and threatened imprisonment; Yusuf chose confinement over the sin she and the women invited him to commit.

TAB-FULL:v13p143/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p143/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p143/r2.claim: Al-sijn means confinement or the prison house. Arabs use place nouns derived from verbs in place of verbal nouns; with fatḥa, sajN is a regular verbal noun.

TAB-FULL:v13p143/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p143/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p143/r3.claim: Although a reading with fatḥa on the first consonant was attributed to some early readers, al-Tabari rejects it because the authoritative readers agree against it.

TAB-FULL:v13p143/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p143/r4.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v13p143/r4.claim: Al-Suddi glosses what they invited Yusuf to as illicit sex.

TAB-FULL:v13p143/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p143/r5.speaker: ابن إسحاق
TAB-FULL:v13p143/r5.claim: Ibn Ishaq says Yusuf sought his Lord's aid and preferred prison to doing what God disliked.

TAB-FULL:v13p145/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p145/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p145/r1.claim: If God does not repel their plotting, Yusuf says he may incline toward them and follow what they desire; ṣabā ilā means to lean or turn toward something.

TAB-FULL:v13p145/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p145/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p145/r2.claim: The cited poetic line uses ṣabā for the heart inclining toward Hind; the verb may also be used transitively in the following hemistich.

TAB-FULL:v13p145/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p145/r3.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v13p145/r3.claim: Qatada explains aṣbu ilayhinna as following the women.

TAB-FULL:v13p145/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p145/r4.speaker: ابن إسحاق
TAB-FULL:v13p145/r4.claim: Ibn Ishaq glosses their plotting as what Yusuf feared from them and his inclination as a response to that danger.

TAB-FULL:v13p145/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p145/r5.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v13p145/r5.claim: Ibn Zayd says that without God's aid and protection, Yusuf could not prevent himself from yielding.

TAB-FULL:v13p146/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p146/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p146/r1.claim: Being among the ignorant means that by inclining to the women Yusuf would join those who disregard God's rights and disobey His commands and prohibitions.

TAB-FULL:v13p146/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p146/r2.speaker: ابن إسحاق
TAB-FULL:v13p146/r2.claim: Ibn Ishaq glosses the phrase as being ignorant through committing God's disobedience.

ZAJJAJ:v3p108/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p108/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p108/r3.claim: Sijn with fatḥa is the verbal noun (‘being imprisoned is preferable’); with kasra it names the prison (‘staying in prison is preferable’).

ZAJJAJ:v3p108/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p108/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p108/r4.claim: Aṣbū ilayhinna means to incline toward them; ṣabā yaṣbū is to be drawn toward amusement.

ZAJJAJ:v3p108/r5.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p108/r5.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p108/r5.claim: Kaydihinna may mean the ruler’s wife alone, using plural for her, or her and the women who saw Joseph.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r1.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r1.claim: Joseph says imprisonment is dearer to him than committing adultery with the women.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r2.speaker: ابن عيينة
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r2.claim: A person is granted supplication only in accord with what is decreed; when Joseph later asked to be remembered, Gabriel showed him an ant gnawing a stone, and God said Joseph had forgotten him and would be kept imprisoned longer.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r3.speaker: ابن اسحاق
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r3.claim: Joseph turned to God and sought his aid, saying prison was preferable to doing what God disliked.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r4.speaker: ابن اسحاق
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r4.claim: Joseph feared the women's scheme and asked God to turn it away from him.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r5.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن اسلم
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r5.claim: Without God's strength and protection, Joseph would have no strength or protection of his own.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r6.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r6.claim: The verb “aṣbu ilayhinna” means to follow the women.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r7.speaker: ابن اسحاق
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2138/r7.claim: If Joseph yielded and committed the sin, he would be ignorant.

NAHHAS:v2p327/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p327/r2.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p327/r2.claim: Prison is easier; Uthman is reported to read السجن with fatḥ; the conditional means Joseph would sin without protection.

THALABI:v5p219/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p219/r10.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p219/r10.claim: Joseph says he may incline toward the women unless God turns their plot away; ṣabā means to lean and long for something.

THALABI:v5p219/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p219/r11.speaker: يزيد بن ضبة
THALABI:v5p219/r11.claim: Yazid ibn Dabba’s line about his heart inclining toward Hind serves as evidence for the meaning of ṣabā.

THALABI:v5p219/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p219/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p219/r8.claim: When she persists and threatens him, Joseph prefers prison to sin and addresses God with a vocative attached to the divine name.

THALABI:v5p219/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p219/r9.speaker: يعقوب
THALABI:v5p219/r9.claim: The common reading has al-sijn with kasra as a noun; Yaʿqub reads it with fatḥa as a verbal noun meaning imprisonment.

THALABI:v5p220/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p220/r1.speaker: يزيد بن ضبة
THALABI:v5p220/r1.claim: Yazid ibn Dabba’s verse that his heart inclined toward Hind illustrates ṣabā as longing or inclination.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p32/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p32/r7.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p32/r7.claim: Yusuf's prayer shows the wife of al-Aziz invited him again after their situation was exposed; his plural address may honor her or avoid speaking of her directly, or refer to the women who admired him.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p32/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p32/r8.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p32/r8.claim: The women's plot may mean the sexual sin urged by al-Aziz's wife or the other women's attempt to attract his heart.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p32/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p32/r9.speaker: قتادة
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p32/r9.claim: Qatada glosses asbu ilayhin as following or complying with the women; another interpretation is that Yusuf would incline toward them, supported by a cited poem.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p34/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p34/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p34/r1.claim: The cited poetic line witnesses the sense of inclination in Yusuf's phrase, 'I would incline toward them.'

QUSHAYRI:v2p76/r7.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p76/r7.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p76/r7.claim: Trial is joined to choice: Joseph chose imprisonment over temptation, and was then tested to prove the truth of his choice.

QUSHAYRI:v2p76/r8.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p76/r8.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p76/r8.claim: Joseph speaks from the eye of unity: salvation required God to turn temptation away, not Joseph’s own effort or avoidance.

QUSHAYRI:v2p76/r9.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p76/r9.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p76/r9.claim: Joseph accepted hardship for God over bodily pleasure, and God later favored him over his brothers.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p106#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p106#2/r1.speaker: أبو بكر
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p106#2/r1.claim: The prayer asks that entering prison be preferable to what the women demand: disobedience and exposure to God's anger; an implied word for entering is omitted.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p106#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p106#2/r2.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p106#2/r2.claim: Al-Zajjāj supports the interpretation that an omitted genitive means entering prison.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p106#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p106#2/r3.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p106#2/r3.claim: Al-Farrāʾ allows السجن to mean imprisonment itself, a verbal noun used in place of the source form, rather than the place of confinement.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p106#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p106#2/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p106#2/r4.claim: One of the two readings is required because سجن with kasra names the prison place, which Joseph cannot mean is itself more beloved than the women's demand.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p106#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p106#2/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p106#2/r5.claim: “More beloved” is an implied comparison: if both choices were desired, prison would be more desirable as the lesser evil and the nearer path to safety.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r1.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r1.claim: The women's plot may refer to the governor's wife alone while encompassing all women, or to her and the women who saw Joseph when she showed him to them.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r2.speaker: وهب
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r2.claim: The women urged Joseph to comply with the governor's wife, accusing him of wronging her and telling him to satisfy her.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r3.claim: أصب إليهن means “I incline toward them.”

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r4.speaker: قتادة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r4.claim: قتادة glosses أصب إليهن as following or yielding to them; the word describes inclining toward desire.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r6.speaker: أهل المعاني
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r6.claim: Alternatively, Joseph fears becoming one deserving blame for ignorance.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r7.claim: Joseph responds to the women's pressure by praying to God and admitting that he could fall into sin unless God protects him; no one avoids sin except by God's grace and protection.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r8.speaker: أبو بكر
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p107/r8.claim: The conditional “unless You turn their plot from me” implicitly means “O God, turn it”; similarly, “unless you obey me, I will punish you” implies an imperative to obey.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:33/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:33/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:33/r1.claim: Joseph prefers prison to the sin to which the women summon him.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:33/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:33/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:33/r2.claim: If God does not divert all the women's schemes, Joseph fears he will incline toward them and become a sinner.

JISHUMI:v5p3637/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3637/r4.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3637/r4.claim: Istʿiṣām is resisting a request to sin; its root means protection or prevention, as in the verse saying there is no protector from God's command.

JISHUMI:v5p3641/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3641/r4.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3641/r4.claim: Turning away from sin comes through God's subtle aid, which is why Joseph prayed and sought God's protection.

JISHUMI:v5p3641/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3641/r5.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3641/r5.claim: A person must seek God's protection when affliction arrives.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r1.claim: The phrase “one of the ignorant” shows that a believer who commits a sin does so out of ignorance.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r9.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r9.claim: Ibn Abbas counts three slips for Joseph: his desire led to prison, asking the cupbearer to remember him prolonged prison, and calling his brothers thieves led them to say his brother had stolen.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239/r1.claim: The invitation may have come only from the wife of the Aziz, with plural wording used indirectly; another view says all the women invited Joseph.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239/r2.speaker: يعقوب
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239/r2.claim: Yaqub alone reads السجن with an open initial سين; the common reading uses kasra.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239/r3.claim: Some say Joseph would not have been tested with prison had he not said prison was preferable; a person is better off asking God for well-being.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239/r4.claim: To incline to the women means to lean toward and follow them; صبا can mean to incline and long for something.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p440#2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p440#2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p440#2/r1.claim: A reading has al-sijn with fatḥ, treating it as a verbal noun; the women collectively urged and adorned compliance while warning him against prison and humiliation.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p440#2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p440#2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p440#2/r2.claim: Yusuf prefers prison to sin because he weighs patient endurance for God, the ugliness of disobedience, and each act's outcome, rather than bodily pleasure and discomfort.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p440#2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p440#2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p440#2/r3.claim: His plea to be turned away from their guile seeks God's subtle help and protection, as prophets and righteous people do while resolving to be patient; it does not ask God to compel chastity.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p440#2/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p440#2/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p440#2/r4.claim: Aṣbu means to incline toward them, with ṣabwah denoting desire; the east wind is called ṣabā because souls incline to its pleasant breeze.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p440#2/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p440#2/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p440#2/r5.claim: A reading derives aṣbu from ṣabābah, passionate yearning.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p440#2/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p440#2/r6.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p440#2/r6.claim: Being among the ignorant may mean failing to act on what one knows, which makes one like the ignorant, or being foolish, since a wise person does not do wrong.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p241/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p241/r4.speaker: الحسن
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p241/r4.claim: When the wife threatened Joseph, the women urged him to obey their mistress and do what she ordered; Hasan gives a similar account, explaining his phrase 'what they invite me to.'

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p241/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p241/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p241/r5.claim: يدعون here has the pattern يفعلن, unlike the masculine plural يدعون.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p241/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p241/r6.speaker: الجمهور
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p241/r6.claim: The majority read السجن with kasra as the noun 'prison'; al-Zuhri, Ibn Hurmuz, Yaqub, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with fatḥa as the verbal noun.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242/r1.speaker: الطبري
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242/r1.claim: The cited poems of Hind and Duraid ibn al-Simma illustrate صبا from الصبوة, youthful inclination or infatuation.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242/r2.claim: The ignorant are those who do not observe God's limits and prohibitions.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242/r3.claim: Joseph's prayer from 'Lord, prison' through 'one of the ignorant' both complains to God about his situation with the women and asks Him to remove the affliction; God's response means granting his wish and preventing the sin by blocking their scheme.

TABRISI:12:30-35#2/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:30-35#2/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:30-35#2/r7.claim: Prison is confinement that prevents a person from acting freely; iʿtiṣām is refraining from sin, while istiʿṣām asks God for protection.

TABRISI:12:30-35/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:30-35/r6.speaker: يعقوب
TABRISI:12:30-35/r6.claim: Yaʿqub alone reads السجن with fatḥa on the sīn, treating it as a verbal noun; the others use kasra for the place-name.

TABRISI:12:33-34/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:33-34/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:33-34/r1.claim: Yusuf says prison is easier to bear than the sexual sin the women invite him to commit; the plural indicates that the women joined the Aziz's wife in inviting him.

TABRISI:12:33-34/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:33-34/r2.speaker: علي بن الحسين
TABRISI:12:33-34/r2.claim: Al-Hasan al-Thumali reports from ʿAli ibn al-Husayn that after leaving the wife, each woman secretly sent to Yusuf asking him to visit her.

TABRISI:12:33-34/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:33-34/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:33-34/r3.claim: One account says the women urged Yusuf to obey their mistress, arguing that she was wronged and he was the wrongdoer.

TABRISI:12:33-34/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:33-34/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:33-34/r4.claim: Another account says the wife let each woman meet Yusuf alone, and each then invited him to herself.

TABRISI:12:33-34/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:33-34/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:33-34/r5.claim: Yusuf does not mean that he positively desires prison: prison is itself sinful if meant as a chosen act, so the phrase means that it is less difficult and easier to bear.

TABRISI:12:33-34/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:33-34/r6.speaker: أبو علي الجبائي
TABRISI:12:33-34/r6.claim: Al-Jubbaʾi reads the phrase as preferring to prepare himself to endure prison rather than prepare himself for adultery.

TABRISI:12:33-34/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:33-34/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:33-34/r7.claim: Yusuf asks God to turn away their scheme through divine لطف, since their scheme had already taken place; ṣabā means inclining to them or their words with desire.

TABRISI:12:33-34/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:33-34/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:33-34/r8.claim: The phrase 'among the ignorant' means either deserving blame for ignorance or acting as though ignorant.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r1.speaker: وهب بن منبه
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r1.claim: Wahb reports that after the women defended her, she asked them to press Joseph to comply; he refused, so she threatened lifelong imprisonment.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r10.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r10.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r10.claim: Alternatively, it may mean Aziz's wife and other women who share her kind of guile.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r2.speaker: يعقوب
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r2.claim: Ya'qub reads al-sijn with fatḥa only here; kasra denotes the place of confinement, while fatḥa denotes imprisonment as an act.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r3.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r3.claim: Al-Zajjaj says the kasra reading means dwelling in prison is preferable to committing sin, while fatḥa means being imprisoned is preferable.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r4.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r4.claim: “Unless You avert their guile” means unless God protects Joseph; “I incline” means I lean toward them.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r5.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r5.claim: The verb ṣabā has forms ṣabwan and ṣabāʾ for inclining toward amusement or desire.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r7.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r7.claim: Although Aziz's wife alone initially schemed, the plural “their guile” has three explanations.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r8.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r8.claim: Arabic can use a plural for one person, as in saying “ships” when someone traveled in only one ship.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r9.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p220/r9.claim: The plural may refer to Aziz's wife and the women who supported her plan.

RAZI-FULL:v18p105#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p105#2/r1.speaker: أهل اللغة
RAZI-FULL:v18p105#2/r1.claim: The word aṣb means to lean or incline toward them; the cited idiom is to incline toward amusement.

RAZI-FULL:v18p105#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p105#2/r2.speaker: أصحابنا
RAZI-FULL:v18p105#2/r2.claim: The theologians argue that a person avoids sin only when God diverts him: whenever one motive prevails, its preference comes from God, and diversion makes sin outweighed.

RAZI-FULL:v18p105#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p105#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p105#2/r3.claim: Joseph had strong incentives toward sin and deterrents to abstaining, so he asked God to create countervailing motives; without them, the motive to sin would prevail.

RAZI-FULL:v18p105/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p105/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p105/r1.claim: After the ruler's wife threatened Joseph with prison and disgrace, the women gathered and pressured him; beauty, wealth, promised gifts, their seduction and threats, and fear of violence all weighed on him.

RAZI-FULL:v18p105/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p105/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p105/r2.claim: Human power alone cannot secure such strong chastity, so Joseph sought God's help and chose prison over their invitation.

RAZI-FULL:v18p105/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p105/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p105/r3.claim: A reading pronounces السجن with fatḥa as a verbal noun.

RAZI-FULL:v18p105/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p105/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p105/r4.claim: Prison's hardship is preferable because sexual pleasure would lead to worldly blame and afterlife punishment, while prison brings worldly praise and lasting reward.

RAZI-FULL:v18p105/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p105/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p105/r5.claim: Though imprisonment is itself a wrong, when forced to choose between two evils, prison is the lesser evil than adultery.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34#2/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34#2/r1.claim: Aṣba means incline and long; Joseph says that without God's help to avoid sin he would lean toward the women and become one of the ignorant sinners.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34#2/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34#2/r2.claim: Being among the ignorant means committing sin and deserving blame, or behaving like the unwise; the plea shows only God's aid keeps a person from sin and condemns ignorance.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r1.speaker: الزجاج والنحاس
QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r1.claim: Prison means entering confinement, with the word for entering elided before prison.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r2.claim: Joseph means prison would be easier than committing sin, not that confinement itself was truly desirable.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r3.claim: A report says God told Joseph that he had confined himself by saying prison was dearer, and that choosing well-being instead would have brought him relief.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r4.speaker: عثمان بن عفان
QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r4.claim: Uthman is said to have read السجن with a fatḥa on the sīn; Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abd al-Rahman al-Araj, and Yaqub are also reported to read it as the verbal noun of imprisonment.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r5.claim: The scheme may mean the women who had seen Joseph and urged him to comply with the Aziz's wife, claiming she was wronged.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r6.claim: Another explanation says each woman privately offered herself under the guise of advising him about the Aziz's wife; Joseph lamented that one woman had become a group.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:33-34/r7.claim: The plural scheme may refer only to the Aziz's wife, using plural address for her importance or as indirect speech instead of naming her explicitly.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:33/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:33/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:33/r1.claim: Yaqub reads al-sijn with fatḥa as a verbal noun; prison is preferable to their sexual invitation because Joseph considers the eventual outcome, despite his natural aversion to prison.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:33/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:33/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:33/r2.claim: The women are all said to invite him because they threatened him for refusing their mistress and adorned submission; alternatively, they each invited him to themselves.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:33/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:33/r3.speaker: قيل
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:33/r3.claim: Another view says imprisonment came upon Joseph because he said this; he should have asked God for well-being, since the Prophet corrected someone who asked for patience.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:33/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:33/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:33/r4.claim: Joseph asks God to turn away the women's schemes by strengthening his protection, because otherwise he would naturally incline to them through desire.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:33/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:33/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:33/r5.claim: Asbu means to incline toward them or their side by natural desire; it is related to sabwah, inclination to desire, and one reading derives it from yearning.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:33/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:33/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:33/r6.claim: Being among the ignorant may mean acting foolishly by doing what they invite, or failing to act on what one knows, since such people are like the ignorant.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p187#3/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p187#3/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p187#3/r1.claim: The women are said to have invited Joseph because they urged him to accept their mistress and each may have privately invited him herself.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p187#3/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p187#3/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p187#3/r2.claim: Joseph turns to God, preferring prison to committing the sin they solicit.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p187#3/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p187#3/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p187#3/r3.claim: His conditional plea asks God to turn their plot away and protect him; aṣbū means incline toward them and desire.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p187#3/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p187#3/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p187#3/r4.claim: Ṣabwa means inclination toward desire and is related to ṣabā, the pleasant breeze toward which souls incline; the ignorant are either those who fail to act on knowledge or the foolish.

QASHANI:12:33/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:12:33/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:12:33/r1.claim: The soul's enduring natural attraction pulls the heart downward, while its illumination and obedience are temporary; without God's protection, the heart's dual nature inclines toward it in ignorance.

QASHANI:12:33/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:12:33/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:12:33/r2.claim: The heart has two natures and faces, one turning toward spirit and the other toward soul; it needs continual divine protection and heavenly light.

QASHANI:12:33/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:12:33/r3.speaker: عليه السلام
QASHANI:12:33/r3.claim: The Prophet repeatedly asks God to keep his heart firm in religion, illustrating its need for protection.

QASHANI:12:33/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:12:33/r4.speaker: عليه السلام
QASHANI:12:33/r4.claim: The Prophet compares the heart to a feather in an open plain turned by the winds, explaining its vulnerability.

QASHANI:12:33/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:12:33/r5.speaker: author
QASHANI:12:33/r5.claim: Joseph's prayer for protection expresses the heart's continual and necessary dependence on God.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p272#2/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p272#2/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p272#2/r10.claim: A variant derives aṣib from ṣabāba, intense longing that pours toward what one desires.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p272#2/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p272#2/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p272#2/r5.claim: The women urge Joseph to obey, framing compliance as preferable to imprisonment and humiliation; his answer attributes the call to them because they counsel and adorn compliance.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p272#2/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p272#2/r6.speaker: عثمان ومولاه طارق وزيد بن علي والزهري وابن أبي إسحاق وابن هرمز ويعقوب
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p272#2/r6.claim: These readers pronounce sijn with an open sīn as the verbal noun of imprisonment.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p272#2/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p272#2/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p272#2/r7.claim: Aḥabb is not a true comparison: Joseph chooses the lesser of two evils, rejecting sinful pleasure for hardship in God's cause, patience, and prayer for relief.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p272#2/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p272#2/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p272#2/r8.claim: Joseph entrusts protection to God and submits, as prophets and the righteous do, since only God averts evil.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p272#2/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p272#2/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p272#2/r9.claim: Aṣbu indicates inclination alone, not committing the forbidden act.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r1.speaker: الجمهور
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r1.claim: The majority derive aṣbu from ṣabā, to turn toward amusement or play; ṣibā with kasra means play.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r2.claim: Al-jāhilīn can mean people whose knowledge produces no benefit or foolish people, since yielding to the women's invitation would be folly; a poem supports the latter sense.

SAMIN-DURR:12:33#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:33#2/r1.speaker: العامة
SAMIN-DURR:12:33#2/r1.claim: The common reading أصب has a light b from صبا يصبو, to incline with longing; الصبوة is desire for passion, and الصبا names the pleasant wind toward which souls incline.

SAMIN-DURR:12:33#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:33#2/r2.speaker: فرقة
SAMIN-DURR:12:33#2/r2.claim: A group doubles the b from صببت صبابة, describing tenderness and intense longing as if love poured into its object like water.

SAMIN-DURR:12:33/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:33/r1.speaker: العامة
SAMIN-DURR:12:33/r1.claim: The common reading has rabbī with kasra for the omitted yāʾ of possession; السجن is the nominative subject and means entering prison.

SAMIN-DURR:12:33/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:33/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:33/r2.claim: On the common reading, السجن is a subject and أحب its predicate; السجن means imprisonment.

SAMIN-DURR:12:33/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:33/r3.speaker: بعضهم
SAMIN-DURR:12:33/r3.claim: Some read رب with a damma and السجن in genitive, taking رب as the subject and meaning that facing the jailer or enduring imprisonment is dearer.

SAMIN-DURR:12:33/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:33/r4.speaker: عثمان ومولاه طارق وزيد بن علي والزهري وابن أبي إسحاق وابن هرمز ويعقوب
SAMIN-DURR:12:33/r4.claim: They read السجن with a fatḥa, making it a verbal noun for imprisonment.

SAMIN-DURR:12:33/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:33/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:33/r5.claim: إلي depends on أحب; the construction is not a true comparative because Joseph never desired what they asked, but chose the lesser of two evils.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p386/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p386/r1.speaker: يوسف
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p386/r1.claim: Joseph prefers prison to the indecency they invite him to; recognizing his dependence on God, he asks to be turned from their plot rather than left to his own weakness.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p386/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p386/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p386/r2.claim: God answered Joseph, turned the women's plot away, and protected him; Joseph chose prison over sin despite youth, beauty, and a powerful, beautiful woman inviting him, seeking God's fear and reward.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p386/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p386/r3.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p386/r3.claim: A report in both Sahih collections says seven types receive God's shade, including a young person raised in worship and a man invited by a beautiful, high-status woman who replies that he fears God.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p34/r10.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p34/r10.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p34/r10.claim: Calling prison more beloved is deliberately paradoxical: Joseph dislikes both options, but says imprisonment is the lesser evil and the women's invitation is more abhorrent.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p34/r11.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p34/r11.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p34/r11.claim: The comparison itself proves the intended meaning: nobody normally loves prison, so the expression of love makes clear that he would prefer it to the worse alternative.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p34/r12.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p34/r12.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p34/r12.claim: Dua is a request addressed upward to one above the speaker, though its form resembles a command addressed downward to a subordinate.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p34/r13.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p34/r13.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p34/r13.claim: If God does not repel their scheme, Joseph may incline toward them because people are naturally susceptible; once chastity is breached, further transgressions follow, and he would become deeply ignorant.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p34/r9.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p34/r9.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p34/r9.claim: Joseph addresses God without a request particle, absorbed in witnessing God, and defends himself against the combined temptations of beauty, rank, wealth, and the women's persuasion.

DURR-FULL:v4p503/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p503/r5.speaker: يوسف
DURR-FULL:v4p503/r5.claim: Joseph says prison is preferable to the sexual sin the women invite him to commit.

DURR-FULL:v4p532/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p532/r3.speaker: ابن عيينة
DURR-FULL:v4p532/r3.claim: Ibn ʿUyayna says success in prayer is granted according to what is decreed; Gabriel showed Joseph an ant gnawing a rock, and God reminded him that He had not forgotten the ant though Joseph had asked for prison.

DURR-FULL:v4p532/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p532/r4.speaker: ابن زيد
DURR-FULL:v4p532/r4.claim: Joseph's plea means that without God's strength and protection, he himself has neither strength nor protection against the women's plot.

DURR-FULL:v4p532/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p532/r5.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v4p532/r5.claim: Qatadah glosses aṣbu ilayhinna as following the women; Ibn Abbas glosses it as complying with them.

DURR-FULL:v4p532/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p532/r6.speaker: عمرو بن مرة
DURR-FULL:v4p532/r6.claim: Anyone who sins deliberately or by mistake is ignorant while committing it; Joseph knew adultery was forbidden and would be ignorant if he followed the women.

BURSEVI:v4p163/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v4p163/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v4p163/r1.claim: The ignorant are those who know but do not act; one who sins this way is no better than an ignorant person.

BURSEVI:v4p163/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v4p163/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v4p163/r2.claim: Alternatively, ignorance means foolishness: the wise person would not commit the indecent act urged on Joseph; adultery belongs to foolish conduct.

BURSEVI:v4p163/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v4p163/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v4p163/r3.claim: Whoever commits adultery has entered the ranks of lying ignoramuses.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p234#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p234#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p234#2/r1.claim: Joseph answers an implied question by privately appealing to God. Al-sijn normally means prison; several readers pronounce it with fatḥa as the verbal noun ‘imprisoning.’

ALUSI-FULL:v12p234#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p234#2/r2.speaker: عثمان
ALUSI-FULL:v12p234#2/r2.claim: ʿUthmān, Ṭāriq, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, al-Zuhrī, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, Ibn Hurmuz, and Yaʿqūb read al-sajn with fatḥa as a verbal noun.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p234#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p234#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p234#2/r3.claim: Joseph says prison is preferable because brief hardship leads to lasting relief; the alternative is compliance with the women and painful punishment. The comparative is not literal since he has no desire for their request.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p234#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p234#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p234#2/r4.claim: Calling prison ‘beloved’ cuts off their hope that fear will make him cooperate; reports say the women threatened him and individually sought him in private.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p234#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p234#2/r5.speaker: علي بن الحسين
ALUSI-FULL:v12p234#2/r5.claim: ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn reports that each woman secretly sent Joseph a request to visit.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p234#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p234#2/r6.speaker: القرطبي
ALUSI-FULL:v12p234#2/r6.claim: Al-Qurṭubī cites a report that God told Joseph prison was his own doing because he asked for it instead of safety; al-Tirmidhī transmits the Prophet’s advice to ask for well-being rather than patience in affliction from Muʿādh ibn Jabal.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p235/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p235/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p235/r1.claim: Joseph asks God to deflect the women’s plot by sustaining his chastity; he attributes good and escape from evil to divine favor rather than his own power.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p235/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p235/r2.speaker: أبو السعود
ALUSI-FULL:v12p235/r2.claim: Abū al-Suʿūd says Joseph admits a natural impulse and pleads like a desperate person: save me or I perish. Al-Qutb and others call this a Muʿtazilī evasion of the Ashʿarī inference that God turns the servant from sin.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p235/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p235/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p235/r3.claim: Illā contracts from in lā, the conditional particle plus negation, with n assimilated into lām; aṣbu is jussive as apodosis, from ṣabā, to incline toward desire.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p235/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p235/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p235/r4.claim: The conditional clause coordinates with ‘prison is dearer’; the nominal first clause expresses an enduring preference. Another reading derives aṣbu from intense yearning that flows toward its object.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p235/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p235/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p235/r5.claim: ‘Among the ignorant’ means those who do not act on knowledge or fools who commit ugly acts; the poetic line uses ignorance to mean folly rather than lack of knowledge.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r1.claim: This explanatory resumption invites the reader to ask how Joseph received the chief wife's demand during an acute crisis.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r2.claim: Joseph's words are a private prayer to God; he may instead have said them aloud to discourage the women.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r3.claim: Most readers pronounce al-sijn with kasra; Yaqub alone uses fatḥa, making it a verbal noun meaning imprisonment.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r4.claim: Joseph preferred prison's pain to unlawful pleasure because it would protect him from sin; his preference is genuine and arises from reflection.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r5.claim: Saying prison is dear is performative contentment with obeying God, not merely information about an inner state.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r6.claim: The relative phrase about what they invite him to hints that social pressure usually makes compliance easier, yet the women's concerted demand did not break his resolve.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p265#3/r7.claim: The plural “they invite me” can mean women's collective desire generally or the gathered women who joined the chief wife's pressure; this parallels the plural in the later plot.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p266/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p266/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p266/r1.claim: Joseph's conditional statement expresses fear and dependence on God, disavowing his own power and fearing that his heart may turn toward forbidden pleasure; it functions as a prayer.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p266/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p266/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p266/r2.claim: Aṣb means to incline toward something beloved; the ignorant are foolish and lack forbearance.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p266/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p266/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p266/r3.claim: “Become one of the ignorant” is stronger than simply “be ignorant,” as with “one of the disgraced.”

TABATABAI:12:22-34#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#2/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#2/r1.claim: Yusuf is not verbally monotheist while practically assigning independent power to causes; every good effect in a created cause is also an act of God.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#2/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#2/r2.claim: Yusuf seeks refuge because sin violates faith's protection: Abraham's descendants who believe without mixing faith with injustice are secure and guided.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#2/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#2/r3.claim: Yusuf is God's owned servant, with no independent power to benefit or harm himself; his indirect wording avoids claiming personal power and emphasizes dependence.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#2/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#2/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#2/r4.claim: He says God made his dwelling good rather than saying the woman honored him, because goodness stresses benefit while honor could imply personal status.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#2/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#2/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#2/r5.claim: Outwardly the episode is a struggle between Yusuf and the woman; inwardly divine love contends with bodily passion, and divine attraction prevails.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#22/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#22/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#22/r1.claim: Law is sustained by faith and noble character, while character grows from monotheism; the good-tree parable maps its root to tawhid, branches to virtues, and fruit to righteous deeds.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#22/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#22/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#22/r2.claim: The ascent toward God comes through true belief, and righteous work suited to that belief raises and sustains it.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#22/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#22/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#22/r3.claim: Because people depend on one another’s varied work, society needs laws that protect rights, distribute the value of work fairly, and prevent the powerful from wronging the weak.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#22/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#22/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#22/r4.claim: Laws need penal rules to deter violations and a governing power to enforce them justly; enforcement requires both knowledge of crimes and strength over offenders.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#22/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#22/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#22/r5.claim: Because people naturally seek their own benefit even at others’ expense, ignorance, negligence, or weak enforcement leaves laws unable to stop wrongdoing.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#23/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#23/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#23/r1.claim: When enforcement is concentrated in a despot, people cannot correct him and laws fail; histories repeatedly show tyrants ruling unjustly.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#23/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#23/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#23/r2.claim: Even just laws and severe penalties cannot prevent violations without virtues such as truthfulness, respect for humanity, justice, dignity, and mercy.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#23/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#23/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#23/r3.claim: He argues that powerful nations’ apparent domestic order may rest on collective exploitation and colonization of weaker peoples, shifting tyranny from individual rulers to nations.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#23/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#23/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#23/r4.claim: Terms such as freedom, honor, justice, and virtue can be emptied of their meanings and used to describe their opposites; laws therefore need ethical foundations.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#23/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#23/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#23/r5.claim: Morality needs belief in one eternal, all-knowing and powerful God, who created perfectly, will judge people, reward good, punish evil, and grant an everlasting outcome.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#23/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#23/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#23/r6.claim: Belief in divine judgment makes awareness of God an inner restraint from crime; without it, people ultimately seek transient worldly pleasure and obey laws for social convenience or reputation.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r1.claim: Praise and reputation cover only important deeds people know about, not secret acts; remembrance is also an implausible reward for self-sacrifice if nothing remains after death.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r2.claim: Neither reputation nor social reasoning can replace monotheism as a restraint from sin, especially in private conduct or acts that observers misread.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r3.claim: Joseph faced betraying his master or being falsely accused by the wife; only his knowledge of God’s presence restrained him.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r4.claim: Religious piety proceeds through fear, hope, or love; the verse about worldly deception and the hereafter’s punishment, forgiveness, and divine approval grounds these motives.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r5.claim: People differ in disposition: most worship from fear of punishment, while others act piously in hope of forgiveness and Paradise.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#25/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#25/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#25/r1.claim: Those who know God worship because He deserves worship, since He owns them and all things; they seek only His face, though they still fear punishment and hope for mercy.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#25/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#25/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#25/r2.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites a saying that the speaker worships God neither from fear of Hell nor desire for Paradise, but because God is worthy of worship.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#25/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#25/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#25/r3.claim: Knowing God through His beautiful names awakens love, since human nature is drawn to beauty and all creation reflects divine beauty and perfection.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#25/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#25/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#25/r4.claim: Created things praise God through their beauty and point to His majesty through their need and imperfection; lovers see them as signs rather than independent realities.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#26/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#26/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#26/r1.claim: Those devoted to love see every created thing as a sign of God; this love purifies them from selfish desires and makes sincerity in worship possible.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#26/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#26/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#26/r2.claim: The author cites a report from Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq that religion is love, and another saying that he worships God out of love for Him.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#26/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#26/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#26/r3.claim: Fear-based worship chiefly motivates avoiding forbidden acts, hope-based worship motivates good deeds, but love directs both toward God Himself and purifies the heart’s attachments.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#26/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#26/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#26/r4.claim: Love makes a person love what God loves, hate what He hates, and accept or oppose things in accordance with God’s approval; it illuminates the path of action.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#27/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#27/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#27/r1.claim: Divine love is the light and spirit that guides a person to good works, explaining why the lover does only what is beautiful and avoids evil.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#27/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#27/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#27/r2.claim: The lover sees every event, great or small, as a sign unveiling absolute beauty and goodness, so worldly afflictions do not produce grief, pain, or fear in the ordinary way.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#27/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#27/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#27/r3.claim: Qur’anic assurances that God’s friends have no fear or grief and that the secure are guided describe this state of joy and safety.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#27/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#27/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#27/r4.claim: The purified, near servants receive unveiling knowledge of hidden realities when the veil between them and God is lifted.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#28/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#28/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#28/r1.claim: The lovers are true trustees who submit to God’s decree and acquire noble character; this is what it means for a servant to make religion sincere for God.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#28/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#28/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#28/r2.claim: God’s making a servant sincere means that the servant’s own sincerity, since all he owns belongs to God, is itself God’s act of choosing him for Himself.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#28/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#28/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#28/r3.claim: Some people are created with sound nature, sharp minds, and pure hearts, attaining sincerity by innate purity rather than effort; these are the Qur’anic purified ones, including prophets and Imams.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#28/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#28/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#28/r4.claim: God gives prophets and Imams knowledge that prevents every sin; infallibility and moral justice both restrain sin, but infallibility makes its occurrence impossible.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#29/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#29/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#29/r1.claim: The cited verses imply that the chosen can still choose shirk, though divine guidance prevents it; the Prophet’s warning likewise presupposes responsibility.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#29/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#29/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#29/r2.claim: An infallible person turns away from sin by personal choice; divine protection relates to that choice as divine enabling does to an ordinary believer’s restraint.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#29/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#29/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#29/r3.claim: Support from the Holy Spirit, the spirit of faith, or resistance to Satan does not remove agency; these are causes operating through the person’s own choice.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#29/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#29/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#29/r4.claim: Some determinists say God diverts people by creating a competing will or sending an angel to overpower their natural inclination, on the premise that God is needed only to originate things.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#29/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#29/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#29/r5.claim: This account conflicts with lived experience: people observe themselves choosing without another cause wrestling against them, and angels or Satan act as a vertical rather than competing cause.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#29/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#29/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#29/r6.claim: The author also rejects the theory as incompatible with the Qur’anic account of monotheism developed throughout the commentary.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#31/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#31/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#31/r7.claim: A report says the women privately invited Joseph to visit; distressed by their approaches, he asked God to divert their guile, and God answered.

TABATABAI:12:22-34/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34/r1.claim: The wife assumes Yusuf will obey because he has long been compliant and circumstances favor her: they are alone, she desires him, and she uses locked doors, seduction, and a commanding invitation.

TABATABAI:12:22-34/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34/r2.claim: Yusuf's heart is absorbed in love of God, leaving no room for another; divine attraction makes him disregard apparent worldly causes and support.

TABATABAI:12:22-34/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34/r3.claim: Yusuf answers only by seeking refuge in God; he does not cite fear of the ruler, prophetic lineage, chastity, reward, or punishment, showing that no other cause occupies his attention.

TABATABAI:12:22-34/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34/r4.claim: Yusuf's refuge in God differs from Mary's words to the apparition: he names God alone, expressing a more complete absorption in divine presence.

TABATABAI:12:22-34/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34/r5.claim: Yusuf says God gave him a good dwelling, recognizing God—not the woman or her husband—as the true source of his care; accepting her invitation would be injustice and cannot lead to success.

TABATABAI:12:32-33#2/r10.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:32-33#2/r10.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:32-33#2/r10.claim: While the women urged him, Joseph neither attended to them nor answered; he turned to his Lord.

TABATABAI:12:32-33#2/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:32-33#2/r8.speaker: الراغب
TABATABAI:12:32-33#2/r8.claim: Al-Rāghib explains ṣabā as yearning and acting like a child.

TABATABAI:12:32-33#2/r9.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:32-33#2/r9.speaker: المجمع
TABATABAI:12:32-33#2/r9.claim: Al-Majmaʿ defines ṣabwah as the delicacy or softness of passion.

TABATABAI:12:32-33/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:32-33/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:32-33/r2.claim: Yusuf was unmoved by the women's beauty, their enticing words, or the threat; he turned only to God, whose beauty and majesty eclipsed all others.

TABATABAI:12:32-33/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:32-33/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:32-33/r3.claim: The group seduction was harder than the earlier private trial: many women openly conspired and threatened him, with circumstances favoring them more strongly than the Aziz's wife alone.

TABATABAI:12:32-33/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:32-33/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:32-33/r4.claim: Because the present trial was more severe, Yusuf prayed for God to ward off their scheme, whereas before he had only sought refuge; God answered and turned their plot away.

TABATABAI:12:32-33/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:32-33/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:32-33/r5.claim: The ending names God as all-hearing and all-knowing, answering Yusuf's prayer and knowing the women's scheme.

TABATABAI:12:33#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33#2/r1.speaker: علي بن الحسين
TABATABAI:12:33#2/r1.claim: A report from Imam al-Sajjād recounts Joseph’s resistance to the wife, the child’s shirt test, the women’s gathering and private approaches, Joseph’s plea for protection, and his eventual imprisonment.

TABATABAI:12:33#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33#2/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33#2/r2.claim: The report’s explanation that Joseph’s household belongs to God supports reading his earlier reference to his Lord as God rather than the Egyptian master.

TABATABAI:12:33#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33#2/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33#2/r3.claim: The report says Joseph refused the women and then uttered the conditional plea, confirming that ‘prison is dearer to me’ was not itself part of a prayer for imprisonment.

TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r1.claim: Joseph’s later wording that he had not betrayed her in his absence, along with the women’s role in the affair, suggests they invited him toward the wife and shared the story with her.

TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r2.claim: It is implausible that the women, after being overwhelmed by Joseph’s beauty, simply left without pursuing him; their conduct helps explain the severity of his ordeal.

TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r3.claim: The conditional wording ‘unless You divert’ signals that Joseph’s sanctifying strength was continuously bestowed, rather than acquired once and thereafter independent of God.

TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r4.claim: God’s response and fresh diversion of their guile indicate a new, ongoing act of divine protection.

TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r5.claim: The protection is knowledge: Joseph calls yielding ignorance, while he describes the same wrongdoing to the wife as injustice and to the king as treachery, framing it in terms they understand.

TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r6.claim: God hears His servants’ words and knows their conditions; thus He answered Joseph by diverting the women’s guile.

TABATABAI:12:33-34/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33-34/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33-34/r1.claim: Joseph is not praying to be imprisoned or asking God to send him to prison to escape temptation; he explains to God that, through divine training, he prefers prison to sin.

TABATABAI:12:33-34/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33-34/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33-34/r2.claim: His words echo his earlier appeal to God when the wife first seduced him: both express reliance on God and resistance through Him.

TABATABAI:12:33-34/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33-34/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33-34/r3.claim: The declaration that prison is preferable prepares for the following conditional plea, which presents itself as a statement of his state.

TABATABAI:12:33-34/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33-34/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33-34/r4.claim: He says he would choose prison if offered the choice, then asks God to divert their guile; without divine protection he would incline to them and fall into ignorant desire.

TABATABAI:12:33-34/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33-34/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33-34/r5.claim: Ahabbu ilayya means he would choose prison over their invitation; it does not show that he positively loved their proposal beyond ordinary human inclination.

TABATABAI:12:33-34/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33-34/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33-34/r6.claim: God’s response concerns the request embedded in the conditional plea to divert their guile, not a request for prison; the next verse explicitly says He diverted their guile.

TABATABAI:12:33-34/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33-34/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33-34/r7.claim: Some took the response as granting a prayer for imprisonment, but the author rejects this: the later wording says only then did they decide to imprison him.

TABATABAI:12:33-34/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33-34/r8.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33-34/r8.claim: The verse does not specify whether the women invited him to themselves, to the wife, or to both; his saying he might incline to them suggests they invited him personally.

TABATABAI:12:33/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33/r1.claim: The purified know God in a way others do not, and divine love makes them seek only God’s will; the verses about Iblis exempting God’s purified servants support this.

TABATABAI:12:33/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33/r2.claim: The verse about God teaching the Prophet supports the author’s claim that infallibility is a form of knowledge that diverts a person from wrongdoing.

TABATABAI:12:33/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33/r3.claim: Unlike ordinary knowledge, this knowledge invariably changes conduct; other people may deny what they know, follow desire despite knowledge, or dispute from envy.

TABATABAI:12:33/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33/r4.claim: Although prophets and Imams conveyed teachings about God’s names and attributes, the verse exempts their descriptions from God’s transcendence beyond ordinary descriptions, showing their knowledge differs in kind.

TABATABAI:12:33/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33/r5.claim: Infallible knowledge does not compel action; it strengthens choice, as someone who knows a drink is deadly freely refuses it.

TABATABAI:12:35/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:35/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:35/r1.claim: The imprisonment begins a period of several years that brings Joseph close to the king and to Egypt’s authority; in prison he calls people to monotheism and first identifies his Abrahamic family.

ASAD-NOTES:12:33#n31/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:12:33#n31/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:12:33#n31/r1.claim: Saba combines inclination with yearning and amorous indulgence, which motivates Asad's rendering of Joseph's feared response.

ASAD-NOTES:12:intro/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:12:intro/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:12:intro/r2.claim: Unlike Genesis' romantic account of Joseph's fortunes, the Qur'anic story illustrates God's unfathomable direction of human affairs: people may hate what is good for them or love what is bad for them.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Zelicha threatened prison to pressure Joseph, but he preferred confinement to committing the evil she demanded.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:33/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:33/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:33/r1.claim: Zulaykha had won the invited women’s support, yet the healthy, handsome Joseph mastered his will and passed one of life’s hardest tests.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:33/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:33/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:33/r2.claim: A key purpose of the story is to model a virtuous young person for Muhammad’s community: despite youth, beauty, opportunity, and desire, he protects chastity through reason, will, and faith in his values.

QIRAAT-ER:12:33:3#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:12:33:3#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:12:33:3#1/r1.claim: Changing kasra on sīn to fatḥa changes the noun pattern, and sajn may carry a verbal-noun sense.

STUDYQURAN:12:33/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:33/r1.speaker: R
STUDYQURAN:12:33/r1.claim: The women backed Zulaykhā’s ultimatum and told Joseph he must obey or face prison.

STUDYQURAN:12:33/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:33/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:12:33/r2.claim: Joseph preferred the Hereafter to fleeting worldly pleasure: illicit surrender meant next-life punishment, while prison meant hardship now and felicity later; human love was real but illicit beside God’s Love.

STUDYQURAN:12:33/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:33/r3.speaker: Kl
STUDYQURAN:12:33/r3.claim: Joseph turned to God in humility.

STUDYQURAN:12:33/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:33/r4.speaker: Qu
STUDYQURAN:12:33/r4.claim: Joseph sought God’s assistance because only God, rather than his own efforts, could save him.
